topic: Thread Design: Ensuring Unjoinability on All Paths via RAII
explanation: Assumption: A `std::thread` object can safely be left to rely on its default destructor behavior. Reality: If a `std::thread` object is joinable (i.e., it represents an active system thread) when its destructor runs, the program is immediately terminated via `std::terminate`. Why It Fails: This termination is often unexpected and bypasses normal exception handling. To use threads safely within RAII wrappers (like `ThreadRAII`), the wrapper must ensure that the underlying `std::thread` is made unjoinable (either by explicitly joining or detaching it) across all possible exit paths (normal return, exceptions, etc.) before the destructor completes.
practical_example: A function that launches a thread and then throws an exception without cleaning up the thread handle will cause the program to crash when the `std::thread` local variable goes out of scope and calls its destructor.
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
